url: /tamias/getting-started.md

# Getting Started

Install tamias, then point it at a package.

## Install

```sh
cargo install tamias
# or from source:
cargo install --git https://github.com/9aia/tamias tamias
# or, from a checkout:
cargo xtask install
```

`tamias` is a native binary — it stays `cargo install`-able because
every `bins[]` shim in the org execs `tamias bin exec` (bootstrap).
Product CLIs (`myco`, `cuora`, `kuda`, …) are *not* cargo-installable:
they ship as tamias packs — `tamias install 9aia:<name>@<version>`.

## Install a package

```sh
tamias install git:9aia/bupha//libraries/ci-gate#main
tamias install 9aia:ci-gate@0.2.0    # named registry — <registry>:<pkg>@<ver>
tamias list
tamias info ci-gate
tamias verify ci-gate        # recompute the payload digest
tamias doctor                # store, cache, git, registry, drivers — all green?
```

## Author and publish

```sh
tamias bundle pack ./my-bundle
tamias publish ./my-bundle            # writes to the default local registry
# or a served registry:
# tamias publish ./my-bundle --registry http://127.0.0.1:8788
```

## Next

* [Architecture](/explanation/architecture)
* [Content types](/explanation/content-types)
* [Security model](/explanation/security) — digests, drivers, `--allow-drivers`
* [Manage project dependencies](/how-to/manage-deps)
* [CLI reference](/reference/cli)

# Tutorial: your first package

A guided walk from a folder to a published, installed, verified package.

## 1. Make a payload

A package is *bytes + a manifest*. Any folder with a `tamias.yaml` is one.

```sh
mkdir -p hello/world
cat > hello/tamias.yaml <<'YAML'
name: hello
version: 0.1.0
type: files
YAML
echo "hi from hello" > hello/world/greeting.txt
```

`type: files` means "the store entry is the whole story" — no driver.

## 2. Pack it

```sh
tamias bundle pack ./hello
# → packed → hello-0.1.0.tgz
```

## 3. Publish it

Serve a registry (any directory works) and publish into it:

```sh
tamias registry serve --addr 127.0.0.1:8788 --dir ~/.local/share/tamias/registry &
tamias publish ./hello --registry http://127.0.0.1:8788
# → published hello@0.1.0
tamias search hello --registry http://127.0.0.1:8788
```

## 4. Install it

```sh
tamias install ./hello
tamias list
tamias info hello
```

`install` resolved the ref, fetched it, cached the payload by content, and
unpacked it into the **install store** under `~/.local/share/tamias`.

## 5. Verify it

```sh
tamias verify hello
# → hello: ok (sha256:…)
```

`verify` recomputes the payload digest and compares it to the recorded
one. Now poke the store and verify again — it should fail:

```sh
echo tampered >> ~/.local/share/tamias/hello@0.1.0/world/greeting.txt
tamias verify hello   # → digest mismatch
```

## 6. Untamper, then keep going

Reinstall to restore, then try a git ref:

```sh
tamias install git:9aia/bupha//libraries/ci-gate#main
tamias info ci-gate    # provenance: source ref, resolved sha, digest
```

## Next

* [How-to guides](/how-to/publish-to-a-registry)
* [Manage project dependencies](/how-to/manage-deps) — `add` + `tamias.lock`
* [Ref grammar](/reference/refs)
* [CLI reference](/reference/cli)

# Tutorial: heal a failing PR with an agent

A guided walk from `tamias install` to a pull request that fixed
itself: red CI → agent session repairs the code → push → green check →
campaign merges. This is the `pr-heal` workflow bundle, verified
end-to-end — every command below ran for real.

You will need: `tamias`, `peregrin`, `sepia`, `lasius`, `bupha`, `gh`
(on `PATH`, authenticated), and a GitHub repo with a CI check.

## 1. Install the bundle

`pr-heal` ships in the 9aia workspace repo:

```sh
tamias install --allow-drivers ~/GitHub/9aia/workspace/workflows/pr-heal
```

`--allow-drivers` is required for `peregrin-bundle` content — the
bundle renders a systemd service through the peregrin provider.

## 2. Deploy it

```sh
tamias deploy pr-heal
```

This writes `~/.config/peregrin/serve/pr-heal.yaml` — a campaign
document that `include:`s the bundle's `main.yaml` and carries a
`config:` block. The loader deep-merges that block over the bundle
defaults, so **this file is where you configure the deployment**:

```yaml
config:
  name: pr-heal
  public_url: https://tamias.luisfuturist.com
  repo: "you/your-repo"                    # required
  webhook_secret_env: "BUPHA_WH_YOU_YOUR_REPO"  # required
  checkout: "$HOME/GitHub/you/your-repo"   # required — local clone
  agent: "devin"                           # sepia agent-config id
  agent_mode: "bypass"                     # see §6 — required
  max_agent_attempts: 3
  ci_check_name: "ci"
  default_branch: "main"
```

If the webhook secret env var is not already in
`~/.config/peregrin/env`, also declare its name under
`capabilities.secrets` in the same file.

> `tamias deploy` regenerates this file — keep a copy of your config
> block and re-apply it after re-deploys.

## 3. Register the webhook

Point a GitHub webhook at the shared campaign listener (the URL your
deployment's tunnel fronts — `https://tamias.luisfuturist.com/hook`
on this one):

* events: `push`, `pull_request`, `check_run`, `status`
* secret: the value behind `webhook_secret_env`, stored in
  `~/.config/peregrin/env` as `BUPHA_WH_<OWNER>_<REPO>`
  (uppercased, `-` → `_`)

```sh
gh api repos/you/your-repo/hooks -f name=web -f 'config[url]=https://tamias.luisfuturist.com/hook' \
  -f 'config[content_type]=json' -f 'config[secret]=…' \
  -f 'events[]=push' -f 'events[]=pull_request' -f 'events[]=check_run' -f 'events[]=status'
```

## 4. Restart and watch it come up

```sh
systemctl --user restart peregrin-campaign
journalctl --user -u peregrin-campaign -f | grep pr-heal
```

Every `peregrin-bundle` renders into the one shared
`peregrin-campaign.service` — ci-gate, docs-deploy and pr-heal
campaigns coexist on a single webhook listener that demuxes by repo.

## 5. Run the loop

Open a PR that breaks CI (the spike used a `SPIKE_BROKEN` marker that
`ci.sh` rejects):

```sh
gh pr create --title 'deliberate CI failure' --body 'pr-heal e2e'
```

Then watch the chain — no polling anywhere, every hop is a webhook or
entity event:

```
push/pull_request webhook → ci-job entity → bupha CI failure
  → status event → pr-heal.check.failed.<sha>
  → lasius worktree @ sha → sepia agent session fixes the tree
  → lasius commit + push HEAD:refs/heads/<pr-branch>
  → CI re-runs → green check → lasius forge pr merge --squash
```

Real observed output from the verified run (PR #3 of the spike repo):

```
{"merge":"9fcfce2c2de642b68fa55b8f013a3dba530ceb04",
 "mergedAt":"2026-11-11T22:48:17Z","state":"MERGED"}
```

Inspect what happened:

```sh
tamias logs pr-heal                          # campaign service logs
tail -f ~/.local/share/peregrin/serve-history/pr-heal.jsonl   # event log
ls ~/.local/share/pr-heal/worktrees           # heal worktrees (auto-removed on success)
cat ~/.local/share/pr-heal/worktrees/attempts/pr-3            # attempt ledger
```

## 6. The agent permission mode — read this

`agent_mode: "bypass"` is not optional decoration: unattended agent
turns cannot answer ACP `session/request_permission` prompts, and
devin's default `accept-edits` mode prompts on shell commands — the
turn deadlocks until timeout (observed live, twice). `bypass`
auto-approves everything, which is acceptable *because* the agent only
ever touches a disposable worktree. `smart` is the safer middle
ground. T-023 added a proper per-session `permissions` policy on the
sepia wire (`sessions.set_permission_policy`, rules over tool kinds) —
the campaign will migrate to it; until then `bypass` is the honest
setting for unattended heals.

## 7. Safety model, honestly stated

* **Verified-sha merge** — the campaign only merges when an open PR's
  *current* `head_sha` equals the sha that went green. A stale green
  finds no PR and skips.
* **Per-PR attempt ledger** — `<worktree_base>/attempts/pr-<n>` caps
  agent runs (default 3), durable across restarts. Over-cap reports
  `attempts.gaveup` and leaves the PR for a human.
* **Per-sha agent lock** — duplicate failure events can't start
  parallel agents on one worktree.
* **Merge conflicts are NOT auto-resolved** — `merge.failed` is
  terminal; conflict → agent-rework is tracked follow-up work.
* **No-diff fixes fail honestly** — the push node commits without
  `--allow-empty`, so an agent that changed nothing errors instead of
  looping CI forever.

## What just happened, architecturally

| hop | owner |
| --- | --- |
| webhook verify, parse, repo demux | peregrin (`github-webhook` driver, `push_refs`/`*_actions` filters) |
| CI job queue → worktree → status | bupha (`ci-job` entity plane) |
| agent session, prompt, permission mode | sepia (`/api/sessions/run` → `prompt_wait`) |
| worktree, commit, push, PR merge | lasius (`vcs`/`forge` verbs — `gh` is the impl) |
| install, deploy, service lifecycle | tamias (this bundle) |

# How to install from a git repo

Point a ref at a repo, an in-repo subdir, and a rev.

## The ref

```
git:9aia/bupha//libraries/ci-gate#main
│   │           │  │               │
│   │           │  │               └─ #ref — branch, tag, or sha
│   │           │  └─ in-repo path (after `//`)
│   │           └─ repo
│   └─ host/org (bare `org/repo` → github.com)
└─ kind
```

* `//` splits repo from the in-repo path — required because nested
  groups make `a/b/c/d` ambiguous.
* Without `//`, a two-segment prefix is the repo; the rest is the path.
* The resolved **commit sha** is recorded in the store regardless of rev.

## Install

```sh
tamias install git:9aia/bupha//libraries/ci-gate#main
tamias info ci-gate        # shows source ref + resolved sha
```

If the package ships its own `drivers/`, add `--allow-drivers` (or
`TAMIAS_ALLOW_DRIVERS=1`) — see [Write a driver](/how-to/write-a-driver).

## Track it in a project

`tamias add` does the same install *and* records the ref in the
project's `tamias.yaml` + resolved entry in `tamias.lock`:

```sh
tamias add git:9aia/bupha//libraries/ci-gate#main
```

See [Manage project dependencies](/how-to/manage-deps) for the full
add/pin/update/lock flow.

## Re-resolve a moving ref

```sh
tamias update ci-gate      # re-resolve + reinstall from the recorded ref
tamias update --all        # every installed package
tamias update --all --json # machine-readable
```

`update` and `pin` refresh `tamias.lock` when the cwd lockfile already
pins the package.

## Repoint the ref

```sh
tamias pin ci-gate git:9aia/bupha//libraries/ci-gate#main~1
```

`pin` rewrites the recorded ref; the payload is untouched until the next
`update`.

## Air-gapped / repeat installs

Git fetches are cached content-addressed under `~/.cache/tamias/fetch`,
keyed by the resolved sha — a repeat install reuses the cache and costs
nothing.

## See also

* [Manage project dependencies](/how-to/manage-deps)
* [Ref grammar](/reference/refs)
* [Tutorial: your first package](/tutorials/first-package)

url: /tamias/how-to/manage-deps.md
---
# How to manage project dependencies

`tamias install` fetches into the store. **`tamias add`** does that *and*
records the ref in your project's `tamias.yaml` (`deps:`) plus a resolved
entry in `tamias.lock` — run it from the project dir, not inside a
package's own source dir (a package's `tamias.yaml` is its package
manifest, a different document).

## Add and lock

```sh
tamias add git:9aia/bupha//libraries/ci-gate#main
tamias add ./local-bundle --allow-drivers   # if it ships drivers/
```

This writes:

* `tamias.yaml` — `deps:` gains the ref (idempotent).
* `tamias.lock` — the resolved record: source ref, resolved sha,
  payload digest.

## Inspect

```sh
tamias list --json
tamias info ci-gate --json
tamias verify ci-gate --json
```

## Update and repin

```sh
tamias update ci-gate     # re-resolve + reinstall from the recorded ref
tamias update --all       # every installed package
tamias pin ci-gate git:9aia/bupha//libraries/ci-gate#main~1
```

`update` and `pin` keep `tamias.lock` honest: if a lockfile exists in
the cwd and already pins the package, its entry is refreshed to the new
record. A missing lockfile — or one that doesn't pin the package — is
left alone (`add` is what creates it).

`update` re-runs the install path, so a package that ships `drivers/`
needs `--allow-drivers` (or `TAMIAS_ALLOW_DRIVERS=1`) again.

## Sync a fresh checkout

`deps:` + `tamias.lock` are a write-only ledger until you reconcile
them — **`tamias sync`** installs the project's whole dep set, the
missing half of the dependency story:

```sh
tamias sync          # install what's missing or drifted
tamias sync --json   # per-dep outcomes as JSON
tamias sync --locked # strict: refuse to move anything the lock pins
```

For each `deps:` ref, sync checks the store entry against the lock
entry (`source_ref`/`resolved`/`digest`):

* **current** — the store record matches the lock; nothing is fetched.
* **installed / reinstalled** — the dep was missing or drifted, so the
  shared install pipeline runs and `tamias.lock` is refreshed (moving
  refs like `#branch` re-resolve, same as `add`).
* **failed** — the dep's install errored; sync keeps going and exits
  non-zero at the end.

Sync **never removes** store entries — the store is global, not
project-scoped, so extraneous packages are `tamias remove`'s job. A
dep that ships `drivers/` needs `--allow-drivers` (or
`TAMIAS_ALLOW_DRIVERS=1`) like `install`/`add`.

Deps that declare `bins[]` deploy them on install like any other
install path — the post-commit deploy lives in the shared pipeline,
so `sync` (and the `sync` op of `tamias serve`, the TUI's sync) lands
a synced pack's commands on `PATH` too. `tamias bin list` shows deploy
state; `tamias bin deploy <pkg>` is the retry path after a collision.

`--locked` is the reproducible-install mode: every dep must already be
`current` per `tamias.lock` + the store. Drift, a missing store entry,
or a dep with no lock entry fails that dep instead of installing or
moving it — the lockfile must already describe the world.

`tamias sync --from-lock` flips the spec: `tamias.lock` entries are
the source of truth — each recorded `source_ref` installs pinned, the
manifest's `deps:` are ignored, and the lock is never rewritten. Use it
for reproducible restores; use plain `sync` to move with your refs.

The same reconcile is available to embedders as the `sync` op of
`tamias serve` (`{"op":"sync","locked":…,"from_lock":…,"allow_drivers":…,"dir":…}` —
`dir` defaults to the server's cwd) and in the TUI's Manifest pane
(`s` or `:sync`, behind a confirm).

## Remove

```sh
tamias remove ci-gate    # drop the store entry; the fetch cache stays
```

`remove` only drops the store entry — it does **not** run the driver's
`uninstall` teardown. For provider-side cleanup use
`tamias uninstall ci-gate` (see
[Provision and service](/how-to/provision-a-service)).

The cache is content-addressed — removing never deletes shared fetch
entries. `tamias cache clean` maintains it separately (`--days <n>`, or
`--all`; the two conflict).

## See also

* [Install from a git repo](/how-to/install-from-git)
* [Ref grammar](/reference/refs)
* [Scripting tamias](/reference/scripting)

---
# How to put a package's binaries on your PATH

A package declares its executable surfaces in the manifest — `bins[]`
entries — or ships a `bin/` payload dir of executables (the layout
release tarballs use). `install` deploys them into the bin dir **by
default**; `tamias bin` is the verb group for inspecting and managing
them explicitly.

## Declare `bins[]` in the manifest

```yaml
name: mycli
version: 1.0.0
type: mycli
bins:
  - name: mycli              # command name on PATH
    shim: cli                # generated front-end
    driver: mycli            # dispatches to tamias-driver-mycli's `cli` verb
  - name: mytool
    payload: tools/bin/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/mytool
```

Two declaration kinds (exactly one of `shim`/`payload` per entry):

* **`shim: cli` + `driver: <kind>`** — tamias writes a tiny shell
  script into the bin dir that execs `tamias bin exec <pkg> <name>
  "$@"`. `tamias` itself is the helper binary, so driver resolution
  stays dynamic — the shim follows `tamias-driver-<kind>` on `PATH` or
  in `<tamias-home>/drivers/` (including drivers the package itself
  just installed). This is how product CLIs ship: the `peregrin`
  pack's `bins: [{name: peregrin, shim: cli, driver: peregrin}]`.
* **`payload: tools/bin/<triple>/<file>`** — a real binary in the
  payload. Only the host triple's file deploys; declaring any triple's
  path resolves to the host's dir at deploy time, and a payload whose
  `tools/bin/` ships platform dirs but none for this host **fails the
  install**. A path without a triple dir (`tools/bin/<file>`) is a
  portable payload bin.

A package may also ship an undeclared `bin/` dir — every regular file
directly under it is linked too (legacy surface, same alias
machinery).

## Authoring a `tools/bin/` payload

The pack side of `payload:` is a plain directory convention — stage
prebuilt executables under `tools/bin/<triple>/<name>` where
`<triple>` is the Rust target-triple spelling (`rustc -vV`'s host, or
`rustup target list` for cross-builds):

```text
mycli/
  tamias.yaml
  tools/bin/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/mytool
  tools/bin/aarch64-apple-darwin/mytool
```

Ship one dir per platform you support; a file directly under
`tools/bin/` (no triple dir) is a *portable* payload bin — same bytes
on every host. The manifest's `payload:` path may name **any**
triple's dir (typically the one you built on): at install time the
triple segment is replaced with the host's, so one manifest serves
every platform. `tamias pack`/`publish` verifies each declared
payload has a shipped counterpart under *some* platform dir — a decl
that matches nothing fails the pack, not the install.

## Deploy, inspect, remove

```sh
tamias install ./mycli            # bins[] deploy automatically
                                 # (sync, `tamias serve` install, and
                                 #  the TUI deploy the same way)
tamias install ./mycli --no-bins  # opt out

tamias bin list                   # every package's bins + deploy state,
                                  # collisions flagged (--json too)
tamias bin deploy mycli           # materialize now (the retry path)
tamias bin deploy mycli --force   # take over conflicting bin paths
tamias bin destroy mycli          # remove this package's bins; pack stays
```

The bin dir is `$TAMIAS_BIN_DIR` → `$XDG_BIN_HOME` → `~/.local/bin`.
Name collisions **warn and last-deploy wins** — never a hard error —
and `bin list` shows which package owns each name. `destroy` (and
`remove`/`uninstall` after dropping the store entry) removes only
artifacts the package owns: shim scripts carry a `# tamias-bin: <label>` marker, payload bins are proven by their link target;
`--force` also clears foreign files at the bin paths.

## Why links survive upgrades

Store entry dirs are versioned (`name@<version>` or a sha label) and a
new version installs to a *new* dir — a link aimed at the raw entry dir
would dangle after `tamias update`. Instead payload bins link through a
stable per-package **alias** — `bin-alias/<name>` as a sibling of the
store root (`$TAMIAS_HOME/bin-alias`) pointing at the current entry
dir — so `<bin>/<file>` → `<alias>/…` keeps resolving across upgrades;
installs and updates retarget the alias automatically. Re-run
`tamias bin deploy` after an upgrade that *adds* or *renames* binaries
— the alias follows, but new payload files need a fresh deploy pass.

On Unix the links are symlinks. On Windows — where symlink creation
needs privileges — the payload file is **copied** instead; re-run
`tamias bin deploy` after upgrades to refresh stale copies (`--force`
also works).

## Upgrading the binary you're running

`tamias update <name>` upgrades a package, but the *running*
executable can't replace itself — a process keeps its old inode even
after the store entry swaps. **`tamias self-upgrade`** closes that
loop for tamias-managed binaries: it detects that the running exe
resolves into the store (directly, or through the `bin-alias`/bin-dir
link chain — a cargo or distro install fails with "not installed via
tamias"), then re-installs the package's recorded source ref, exactly
like `tamias update`. The install retargets the alias, so the *next*
invocation runs the new version; this process keeps the old one —
restart to pick it up.

```sh
tamias self-upgrade --check   # current vs what the ref resolves to
                              # — no install, fetches to the cache only
tamias self-upgrade           # update + retarget the alias
```

A release install pinned to a `#sha256:` ref re-fetches exactly those
bytes; a moving ref (branch, `latest`) re-resolves. `--allow-drivers`,
`--no-bins`, and `--json` behave as they do for `install`/`update`. On
Windows — where payload bins are copied rather than symlinked — the
running exe file can be locked; self-upgrade warns before attempting
and you may need to close other tamias processes and retry.

## Producing the tamias self-package

The tarball a self-upgrade consumes is built by the repo itself:

```sh
cargo xtask pack-self          # release-build → target/pack-self/tamias-<ver>.tgz
cargo xtask pack-self --skip-build --out /tmp/pkg   # reuse target/release/tamias
```

The verb release-builds `tamias`, stages a `type: files` package
(`tamias.yaml` + `bin/tamias`, version read from
`crates/tamias-cli/Cargo.toml`), and packs it through the same
`tamias-publish` path as `tamias bundle pack`. It prints the tgz's
sha256 and a ready-to-paste pinned install ref — host the tgz
somewhere (e.g. `tamias.9aia.com`) or drop it into a registry payload
dir for `tamias publish`.

## Errors you'll see

* `package 'x' is not installed` — install it first (`tamias install`).
* `<label>: nothing to deploy — no bins[] and no bin/ payload` — the
  package ships no executable surfaces; nothing to do.
* `<path> already exists — refusing to overwrite (use --force)` —
  something else owns the bin path. `bin list` shows the current owner.
* `… is not a tamias-managed binary` (`self-upgrade`) — the running
  exe wasn't installed via tamias; use your package manager or
  `cargo install` instead.

url: /tamias/how-to/use-the-tui.md
---
# How to use the TUI

`tamias ui` opens an interactive console — the same operations as the
CLI verbs, without memorizing flags. It needs the `tui` cargo feature
(on by default; `cargo install tamias --no-default-features` builds the
lean binary without it).

```sh
tamias ui
```

## Panes

`Tab` / `1`–`5` switch between five panes:

* **Installed** — every store entry: name, type, source ref, resolved
  sha, digest, size. `Enter` opens a detail view (manifest, provenance,
  provider services); `Esc`/`←` goes back.
* **Registry** — search-as-you-type against a registry (debounced;
  `Enter` fires immediately). `/` edits the query, `i` installs the
  selected result. `:registry <name>` picks the target — a configured
  registry name or a raw dir/http ref; bare `:registry` resets to the
  default routing.
* **Services** — installed packages' `provider:` services with unit
  state. `s`/`S` start/stop, `r` restart, `e`/`E` enable/disable,
  `d` deploy, `x` uninstall (all confirmed). `t`/`T` tail/follow the
  journal, `n` runs the service in the foreground — `x` kills a live
  stream.
* **Manifest** — the project manifest's `deps:` as an editable table:
  `a` add a ref, `d`/`x` remove, `e` edit (installs the new ref, then
  swaps — a failed install leaves the manifest untouched). Writes go
  through the same manifest+lock path as `tamias add`. `s` (or
  `:sync`) reconciles the whole `deps:` set — `tamias sync`'s
  install-missing-or-drifted pass, behind a confirm.
* **Author** — `p` packs a payload dir (`bundle pack`), `P` publishes
  (dir + registry prompts, confirmed); `r` lists configured registries.

## Keys

Vim-style, same conventions as `myco ui`:

| Key | Action |
| --- | --- |
| `j`/`k`, arrows | move |
| `/` | filter (Installed) / query (Registry) |
| `i` | install-by-ref prompt (Installed) / install result (Registry) |
| `v` `u` `U` `p` `r` `c` `C` `d` | verify · update · update-all · pin · remove · cache clean (>30d) · cache clean all · doctor |
| `:` | command line — `:install <ref>`, `:remove`, `:verify`, `:update`, `:pin`, `:search <q>`, `:registry`, `:run`, `:logs`, `:service`, `:services`, `:deploy`, `:manifest`, `:sync [--from-lock]`, `:pack`, `:publish`, `:registries`, `:clean`, `:doctor`, `:reload`, `:help`, `:q` |
| `?` | help overlay |
| `R` | reload |
| `q` / `Ctrl-C` | quit (kills any live service stream) |

Mutating verbs ask `y`/`n` first (default `n`). Installs that ship
bundled `drivers/` raise the consent prompt — answering `y` is the
equivalent of `--allow-drivers`; there is no env-var shortcut in the
TUI.

## Notes

* Long ops (install, publish, verify) run on a worker thread; phases
  stream into the log strip with a spinner in the status bar.
* The TUI watches the store root and reloads when it changes on disk —
  installs from other terminals show up without `R`.
* Everything the TUI does is also available as CLI verbs or
  `tamias serve` ops — the TUI is a front-end, not a second engine.

---

---
url: /tamias/how-to/publish-to-a-registry.md
---
# How to publish to a registry

Publish a packed package into a registry — a local directory, or a
Cloudflare Worker (R2 blobs + D1/KV index).

## Local registry

```sh
tamias registry serve --addr 127.0.0.1:8788 --dir ~/.local/share/tamias/registry &
tamias publish ./hello --registry http://127.0.0.1:8788
tamias search hello --registry http://127.0.0.1:8788
```

`registry serve` is an **open dev server** — anyone who can reach the
port can read and write the index. Set `TAMIAS_REGISTRY_SERVE_TOKEN`
before serving and clients must send `Authorization: Bearer <token>`
(the client's token comes from `TAMIAS_REGISTRY_TOKEN`).

Without `--registry`, `publish` writes to the default local directory.

## Consume it

```sh
tamias install ./hello                     # a path
tamias install https://host/hello-0.1.0.tgz#sha256:<hex>
```

Digest-pin the tarball (`#sha256:<hex>`) when you have the bytes.

With a **named registry** in config (`tamias registry add`, see below),
install by name — `<registry>:<package>@<version>`:

```sh
tamias install 9aia:hello@0.1.0
tamias install 9aia:@acme/scoped@2.0.0    # scoped package
```

The label matches the registry's `id` (`registry add --id`) first,
then its name; `@<version>` is required. The same refs work in a
project `tamias.yaml`'s `deps:` for `tamias sync`.

## Cloudflare registry

1. Write the Worker + config:

   ```sh
   tamias deploy-registry --out ./tamias-registry-worker
   ```

2. Deploy the Worker with your Cloudflare account and bind R2 + D1/KV.

3. Name the registry once — globally so every project sees it:

   ```sh
   tamias registry --file ~/.config/tamias/tamias.toml add 9aia \
     --kind cf --url https://tamias-registry.you.workers.dev \
     --token-env TAMIAS_REGISTRY_TOKEN
   ```

   (`--file` sits on `registry`, before the subcommand; inside a project
   drop it to write that project's `tamias.yml` instead — the user-level
   file is the base layer a project `tamias.yml` overlays per-field.)

4. Route publish/search at it by default — add to the same file:

   ```toml
   [publish]
   default = "9aia"

   [search]
   default = "9aia"
   ```

5. Publish + search through it — no `--registry` needed:

   ```sh
   export TAMIAS_REGISTRY_TOKEN=…   # the env var NAMED by token_env
   tamias publish ./hello
   tamias search hello
   ```

The protocol is the same either way: the client does a read-modify-write
of `index.json`; the server is a token-guarded blob store (`GET`/`PUT
/<key>`). Auth is a bearer token — the config `token_env` field names
the env var that carries it; clients honor `token_env` (falling back
to `TAMIAS_REGISTRY_TOKEN`). Never inline a token.

## Retention — pruning old versions

Every publish can prune the package's older **index** entries so a
registry doesn't accumulate versions forever (P-024). Configure it in
`tamias.yml`:

```yaml
retention:
  keep: 10                      # versions kept per package
  packages:                     # optional per-package overrides
    "big-*":
      keep: 50
```

`keep` counts versions in **semver order** (prereleases included —
`1.0.0-rc.1` sorts below `1.0.0`), not publish order, and applies per
`(scope, name)`. The version being published is never pruned, and
versions that aren't semver are never pruned either. A `retention:`
block under `registries.<name>` overrides the global policy for that
registry. `tamias publish --keep N` overrides per invocation, and
`tamias publish --json` reports the pruned labels.

Pruning is **index-entry only**: the `.tgz` payload blobs stay in the
registry, but a pruned version no longer resolves through the index —
`search` won't list it and `cf:<name>@<version>` installs can't resolve
it (the `cf:` source reads `index.json`). A direct fetch of the blob
URL still works, and installed copies on consumer machines are
untouched — `verify` recomputes the payload digest locally. Unset
`keep` = keep everything (the default).

## See also

* [Config reference](/reference/config)
* [Tutorial: your first package](/tutorials/first-package)

url: /tamias/how-to/provision-a-service.md

# How to provision and service-manage a package

`install` puts a payload in the store. **Deploy** has two halves:

* the package's **kind driver** (`tamias-driver-<type> deploy`) —
  kind-specific setup/teardown tamias never interprets;
* the manifest's declarative **`provider:` block** — tamias-native
  service/runtime spec that `tamias deploy` materializes itself.

`provider.services[]` renders one **per-user service** per entry — no
driver needed, for any content type (including `files`). The backend
is picked by platform (`tamias_provider::ServiceBackend`): **systemd
user units** on Linux, **launchd LaunchAgents** on macOS
(`~/Library/LaunchAgents`, `gui/<uid>` domain), and **Task Scheduler
tasks** on Windows (`schtasks`, `%LOCALAPPDATA%\tamias\tasks`). All
three render the same `ServiceSpec`; each backend documents its honest
gaps (e.g. Task Scheduler caps restart count, launchd has no
`Description=`/env-file keys — a wrapper script covers `env_file`).

## Declare the provider in the manifest

```yaml
name: ci-gate
version: 1.0.0
type: peregrin-bundle
provider:
  name: ci-gate                  # unit-name prefix; defaults to the package name
  services:
    - name: ci-gate              # service suffix → <provider>-<service>
                                 # (.service on systemd; label/task elsewhere)
      exec: "peregrin campaign serve /srv/ci --port '2917 3'"  # argv string
      env_file: "~/.config/peregrin/env"   # EnvironmentFile=- (optional)
      env: {PORT: "29173"}                 # inline env — secrets stay in env_file/keyring
      workdir: "~"                         # quote a bare ~ (YAML null otherwise)
      restart: on-failure                 # Restart=, default on-failure
  ingress:
    - public_url: https://ci.example.com
      listen: 127.0.0.1:29173
      path: /hook
      hooks:                   # declarative forge hooks — driver deploy consumes these
        - forge: github
          repo: 9aia/peregrin
          events: [push]
  verbs: [run, logs, health]   # advisory CLI hints
  health: {cmd: "curl -sf localhost:29173/health"}
```

Every field is optional; no `provider:` block means nothing to deploy —
today's behavior. `Manifest::validate` rejects malformed specs (a
service without a name or `exec`, duplicate service names, line breaks
in single-line fields, hooks missing `forge`/`repo`).

### What `exec` means

`exec` is a **command line split into argv** — not a shell command.
`tamias` splits it with a small POSIX-ish subset: whitespace separates
arguments, `'…'` is literal, `"…"` allows `\"`/`\\`, and `\c` escapes any
character outside quotes. `$VAR`, globs, pipes, and `#` comments are
*not* expanded — the string is data. Each argv element is then quoted
for `ExecStart=` (systemd double-quote rules), so an argument with
spaces survives intact:

```yaml
exec: "/usr/bin/gate serve --name 'two words' --flag=\"a b\""
# → ExecStart=/usr/bin/gate serve --name "two words" --flag="a b"
```

An unterminated quote or an empty argv fails the deploy.

### Unit rendering (systemd — the Linux backend)

On Linux each `provider.services[]` entry becomes
`<provider.name-or-package>-<service>.service` under
`~/.config/systemd/user` (`$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/systemd/user`). The macOS
and Windows backends render the same fields into a launchd plist
(+ optional `.sh` env-file wrapper) and a Task Scheduler `.cmd`/`.xml`
pair respectively — see each `tamias-deploy-*` crate's docs for the
per-field mapping.

* `After=`/`Wants=network-online.target`;
* `Type=simple`, `Restart=` (default `on-failure`), `RestartSec=5`;
* `EnvironmentFile=-<env_file>` — the `-` makes a missing file
  non-fatal;
* `Environment=K=V` per `env` entry, `WorkingDirectory=` per `workdir`;
* `~`/`~/…` in `workdir` and `env_file` expands to `$HOME` at render
  time — **quote it in YAML** (`workdir: "~"`); a bare `~` parses as
  null.

Unit names are deterministic: `provider.name` wins, else the package
name (scope-qualified — `@ci/gate` → `ci-gate-…`). Two packages claiming
the same unit name resolve last-deploy-wins.

A shared unit name is a feature, not just a collision: packages that
declare the same `provider.name` + service name render **one** unit —
the canonical shape is several content bundles joining a single host
process (e.g. `peregrin-bundle`s whose `campaign` service runs
`campaign serve <dir>` over a directory of generated configs — one
bundle's deploy drops its config there, the host serves them all).
Keep `exec` (and `env_file`/`workdir`) identical across declarers —
last deploy wins the unit file. `uninstall` re-renders a still-shared
unit from a surviving declarer instead of dropping it; only the last
declarer's removal removes the unit.

## Deploy an installed package

```sh
tamias install git:9aia/bupha//libraries/ci-gate#main
tamias deploy ci-gate                       # driver deploy + render provider.services units
tamias deploy ci-gate --config ./node.yaml   # operator params ride a config file
```

`deploy` runs the kind driver's `deploy` verb *and* writes every
`provider.services[]` service through the platform backend (then a
best-effort reload — `systemctl --user daemon-reload` on systemd, a
no-op elsewhere). Services are **not enabled** — activation stays
explicit:

```sh
tamias service enable ci-gate-ci-gate   # systemd: enable --now; launchd:
                                        # bootstrap; Windows: schtasks /change
tamias service status ci-gate-ci-gate    # per-backend status probe
tamias service logs   ci-gate-ci-gate   # journalctl / launchd log tail /
                                        # schtasks snapshot, per backend
```

A package that ships its own `drivers/` needs `--allow-drivers` at
install time (or `TAMIAS_ALLOW_DRIVERS=1`) — the consent gate is
described in [Security model](/explanation/security).

If neither a driver nor `provider.services[]` applies, `deploy` reports
`nothing to deploy (type …)` and succeeds. `uninstall` runs the driver's
teardown, removes the declarative units (best-effort per unit — a unit
another installed provider still declares is re-rendered from the
survivor instead), then drops the store entry; with no driver it warns
that provider-side resources may remain. When the manifest declares `ingress[].hooks[]`,
`deploy` prints a hint pointing at `tamias driver exec <pkg> hooks
register --dry-run` — hook registration stays explicit (the
`public_url` fronts a tunnel the operator confirms first).

## Run provider verbs through the driver

The lifecycle verbs (`install`/`deploy`/`uninstall`) aren't the whole
surface — a driver may declare extra ops verbs in `capabilities.verbs`
(`hooks`, `health`, `status`, …). `tamias driver exec` is the generic
passthrough:

```sh
tamias drivers --json                        # each driver's declared verbs
tamias driver exec ci-gate hooks register --dry-run
tamias driver exec ci-gate hooks register    # real run — forge API + secrets
tamias driver exec ci-gate hooks unregister
tamias driver exec ci-gate health            # JSON status probe
tamias driver exec ci-gate status            # per-unit is-active/is-enabled
tamias driver exec ci-gate logs --lines 50
```

The verb plus everything after it passes through verbatim after the
standard `--dir`/`--name` flags (add `--config <file>` before the verb's
args to forward a node config). The driver's stdout/stderr stream back.
`tamias run` stays the *local* service-exec surface — provider-specific
ops that need the driver's context (manifest secrets, forge API, unit
state) go through `driver exec` instead. `tamias deploy` never
auto-registers ingress hooks: `public_url` fronts a tunnel the operator
confirms, so registration is always an explicit, reviewable step.

## Inspect providers

```sh
tamias provider list          # installed packages' provider: blocks
                              # (services + unit state, ingress, verbs)
tamias provider list --all    # include packages without a provider:
tamias provider list --json   # machine-readable
```

Each service row shows its rendered unit name (`<provider>-<service>`
— `.service` on systemd, a launchd label or task name elsewhere) and a
best-effort enable-state probe (`-` when the backend can't answer).
Ingress rows carry the `public_url` (+ `listen`/`path`).

## Run a service without a service manager

`tamias run` execs a provider service's `exec` argv **in the foreground** —
the same argv/env the rendered unit would get, minus the backend:

```sh
tamias run ci-gate            # sole service → runs it
tamias run ci-gate web        # pick one of several
tamias run ci-gate web -- --port 29174   # extra argv after `--`
```

The child gets a scrubbed environment (parent credentials never leak —
see [Security model](/explanation/security)): the service's `env` plus
its `env_file` parsed as `K=V` lines (inline `env` wins, matching
systemd's `EnvironmentFile` → `Environment=` order). `workdir` (`~`
expands) is the cwd, else the payload dir. A non-zero exit fails the
command. This is the dev/no-service-manager counterpart of
`service enable` — `provider.health.cmd` probes and richer verbs are
still on the roadmap.

## Follow a service's logs

```sh
tamias logs ci-gate            # ALL the package's units, one stream
                               # (journalctl / launchd log tail / schtasks)
tamias logs ci-gate --lines 50 -f
tamias logs ci-gate-ci-gate    # or a bare unit name
tamias service logs ci-gate-ci-gate   # unit-level, same backend stream
```

A package name resolves to every `provider.services[]` unit in one
stream; anything that isn't an installed package is treated as a unit
base name.

## Manage an ad-hoc service

The per-user service mechanism also works without a package — same
verbs, same platform backend:

```sh
tamias service install --unit ci-gate \
  --exec "/usr/local/bin/ci-gate run --flag 'a b'" \
  --env-file ~/.config/ci-gate/env \
  --description "ci-gate" \
  --env HOME=/home/me \
  --restart on-failure \
  --workdir /srv/ci-gate
tamias service enable  ci-gate
tamias service status  ci-gate
tamias service logs    ci-gate
tamias service disable ci-gate
tamias service uninstall ci-gate
```

`service install` writes the unit (it does **not** enable it). `uninstall`
disables + removes the unit file.

## Tear down

```sh
tamias uninstall ci-gate    # driver teardown + unit removal + drop the store entry
```

## See also

* [Write a driver](/how-to/write-a-driver)
* [Content types](/explanation/content-types)

url: /tamias/how-to/deploy-a-ci-gate-bundle.md
---
# How to deploy a CI gate bundle

A `type: bupha` bundle is a CI fleet shipped as tamias content: the
payload carries a `fleet.toml` (the watched repos + runners) and a
`tamias.yaml` manifest whose `provider:` block declares the systemd
units. This guide stands up the org gate bundle — `ci-gate` from
`9aia/bupha` — end to end. The same steps apply to any `type: bupha`
bundle (e.g. `docs-deploy`).

## Install the driver pack

The bundle's driver, `tamias-driver-bupha`, ships as a payload bin in
the bupha product pack (`libraries/bupha`, `type: files`). Install it
first — the bundle's `deploy`/`hooks`/`health`/`status`/`logs` verbs
all dispatch through it.

The driver binary is a build artifact (`drivers/bin/<triple>/` is
gitignored), so install from a checkout, not a `git:` ref:

```sh
cd 9aia/bupha && ./scripts/pack.sh   # release-builds tamias-driver-bupha
tamias install --allow-drivers ./libraries/bupha
```

(`tamias bundle pack libraries/bupha` produces a `.tgz` for hosts that
shouldn't build — install that ref the same way.) `--allow-drivers`
is the consent gate for packages that ship `drivers/` payloads — see
[Security model](/explanation/security). The driver lands in
`~/.local/share/tamias/drivers/`; the provider units exec it by that
absolute path because systemd's minimal `PATH` can't resolve a bare
`tamias-driver-bupha`.

## Install and deploy the bundle

```sh
tamias install git:9aia/bupha//libraries/ci-gate#main
tamias deploy ci-gate
```

`deploy` does two things:

1. Runs the kind driver's `deploy` verb, which merges the bundle's
   `fleet.toml` with the manifest's `provider.ingress` block and writes
   the operator config to
   `~/.config/bupha/bundles/ci-gate.toml` — one file per bundle, under
   `~/.config/bupha/bundles/`. The fleet itself (`[[repo]]` set,
   `[runner]`, `[status]`, `[worker]`) lives in the payload's
   `fleet.toml`; only the manifest-owned fields (`tunnel.public_url`,
   `trigger.listen`/`kind`) come from `tamias.yaml`.
2. Renders each `provider.services[]` entry as a per-user unit named
   `<provider.name>-<service>` — for ci-gate that's
   `bupha-watch.service` and `bupha-worker.service` (see
   [Provision and service](/how-to/provision-a-service) for the unit
   rendering contract).

## Pick an ingress mode — enable ONE service

ci-gate declares two services, one per ingress mode:

| unit | verb | mode |
| ---- | ---- | ---- |
| `bupha-watch.service` | `tamias-driver-bupha host --config ~/.config/bupha/bundles/ci-gate.toml` | standalone: the bundle's own webhook listener (`provider.ingress`) → queue → pipeline. For hosts with no peregrin. |
| `bupha-worker.service` | `tamias-driver-bupha worker --config ~/.config/bupha/bundles/ci-gate.toml` | substrate: polls `kind="ci-job"` entities on the peregrin node named by `[worker] node` in the generated config. For deployments where the ci-ingress campaign owns webhook ingress. |

Enable exactly one — both at once fight over the listener port and
double-run pushes:

```sh
# standalone mode
tamias service enable bupha-watch

# substrate mode (the org's production shape)
tamias service enable bupha-worker
```

A substrate-mode bundle still declares `provider.ingress` — it is the
standalone fallback and the source of `tunnel.public_url` /
`trigger.listen` in the generated config — but only the worker unit
runs.

## Register the forge hooks

`provider.ingress[].hooks[]` is declarative: `tamias deploy` prints a
hint but never registers live hooks. Registration is an explicit
reviewable step:

```sh
tamias driver exec ci-gate hooks register --dry-run   # show the plan
tamias driver exec ci-gate hooks register             # upsert GitHub webhooks
```

For the substrate mode the webhook URL fronts the peregrin campaign
listener instead — the ci-ingress bundle's own `github-webhook` node
owns `repos[]`, so no `hooks[]` are registered from tamias at all.

## Operate the fleet

```sh
tamias provider list                 # provider: blocks + unit state
tamias driver exec ci-gate health    # JSON probe (listener + unit)
tamias driver exec ci-gate status    # per-unit is-active/is-enabled
tamias driver exec ci-gate logs --lines 50
tamias logs ci-gate                  # journalctl over both units
tamias run ci-gate worker            # foreground exec, no service manager
tamias uninstall ci-gate             # units + bundles/ci-gate.toml + store entry
```

The driver's full verb set is `install`/`deploy`/`uninstall`/`hooks`/
`health`/`status`/`logs`/`host`/`worker`/`config-schema` —
`tamias driver exec` passes the verb through verbatim, and
`tamias driver config-schema ci-gate` prints the JSON Schema of the
operator config `deploy` writes. For the entity-plane worker's
`[worker]` block (`node`, `node_token_env`, `labels`) and the
`runsOn` routing it feeds, see bupha's
[distributed runners](https://github.com/9aia/bupha) docs.

Secrets are env-var **names** only — `secret_env`/`token_env` in
`fleet.toml` resolve env → cuora (`cuora://bupha/<NAME>`) → keyring.
Seed values with `printf '%s' "$VALUE" | cuora put cuora://bupha/<NAME>`;
never write a secret into either file.

---

---
url: /tamias/how-to/write-a-driver.md
---
# How to write a content driver

A **driver** teaches tamias how a content *type* installs, deploys, and
uninstalls — with **no compile-time coupling**. tamias discovers
`tamias-driver-<type>` on `PATH` or `<tamias-home>/drivers/` and runs
it as a subprocess.

## The contract

```text
tamias-driver-<type> <verb> --dir <dir> --name <name> [--config <file>]
```

| verb | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `install` | materialize the payload at `--dir` |
| `deploy` | activate (unit, hooks) |
| `uninstall` | tear down — **last installed version only** (see below) |
| `capabilities` | print `{"types":[…],"verbs":[…]}` on stdout — the types + verbs this binary handles |

`uninstall` is **version-aware**: drivers key shared operator state
(`~/.config/<product>/…`) on `--name` alone, so tamias dispatches the
verb only when the store entry being removed is the *last* installed
one sharing that package name. Removing one of several coexisting
versions skips the verb entirely (the store entry still drops, and
the skip is reported); the final removal runs it once, with that
last entry's `--dir`. If your driver tracks per-version resources,
note they accumulate until the last uninstall — keep `uninstall`
cheap and name-keyed.

## Ops verbs beyond the lifecycle three

`install`/`deploy`/`uninstall` are the only verbs tamias dispatches on
its own. A driver may declare **provider ops verbs** — `health`,
`status`, `hooks register`, anything the product needs — by listing them
in `capabilities.verbs`; the operator reaches them through the generic
passthrough:

```sh
tamias driver exec <pkg> <verb> [args…]
# → tamias-driver-<type> <verb> --dir <dir> --name <name> [--config <f>] [args…]
```

Everything after `<verb>` lands verbatim as trailing argv, so verbs can
take their own flags (`--dry-run`, `--api-base`, …). The driver's
stdout/stderr stream back — status/probe verbs should print JSON or
report lines. `tamias drivers --json` shows each driver's declared
verbs; `tamias driver exec` warns (but still dispatches) when the verb
isn't declared — the driver stays the authority. Provider verbs that
answer with data are the right place for forge-hook registration,
health probes, and unit status; `tamias run` remains local service exec
only.

`--config` is an optional path to a node/config file carrying operator
params (`tamias deploy --config`). Exit zero on success; a non-zero
exit fails the tamias verb, with your stderr surfaced. Dispatch has a
120s timeout (`capabilities` probes get 10s), so a hung driver fails the
verb instead of wedging it.

## Operator overrides (`TAMIAS_DEPLOY_OVERRIDES`)

If your driver **generates** operator config (node yaml, service
definitions), regeneration wipes hand-applied edits on every
`install`/`deploy`/`uninstall`. tamias provides a persistence channel —
you own the merge because only you know the generated document's
shape:

* When the package has drop-ins, tamias sets
  `TAMIAS_DEPLOY_OVERRIDES=<dir>` on the driver spawn — every
  lifecycle verb and `driver exec` passthrough carries it.
* `<dir>` is `deploy.d/<kind>/<name>/` under the tamias config root
  (`$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/tamias` → `~/.config/tamias`; `$TAMIAS_DEPLOY_D`
  overrides the root). It holds `*.yaml`/`*.yml`/`*.json` fragments —
  partial documents merged in **sorted-filename order, later files
  win**, with `tamias_core::merge_values` semantics (dicts per-key,
  arrays concat high-first with `id` dedupe).
* Operators write fragments by hand, or use
  `tamias deploy <pkg> --set key=value` (repeatable; dotted keys,
  YAML values → the `cli.yaml` fragment), `--unset`,
  `--clear-overrides`, `--show-overrides`.

To honor it, fold the fragments over your generated doc before
writing — parse each file (YAML or JSON by extension), merge them in
filename order, then `merge_values(overrides, generated)` so operator
keys win. A malformed fragment should fail the verb, not be skipped.
Drivers that generate no config can ignore the variable entirely.
Reference impl: `peregrin-cli`'s `provision` module
(`apply_deploy_overrides`).

## Capabilities

tamias maps a package's `type:` to a driver. Naming the binary
`tamias-driver-<type>` is enough — tamias tries that name first. A
differently-named binary can still claim types by answering
`capabilities`:

```sh
#!/bin/sh
if [ "$1" = capabilities ]; then
  echo '{"types":["myco-config"]}'
  exit 0
fi
# …handle install/deploy/uninstall…
```

## Ship it with the payload

Drop the driver under `drivers/` in your payload — two forms:

* `drivers/<name>` — a portable file (an interpreted script like
  `#!/usr/bin/env python3` ships as source);
* `drivers/bin/<target-triple>/<name>` — a compiled driver, one dir
  per rustc target triple (`x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu`, …). Only the
  host triple's file installs; a package that ships platform dirs but
  none for this host **fails the install** rather than silently
  dropping the driver.

Either way this makes the package **self-modifying**: a bundled driver
is arbitrary code that runs on the installer's machine. tamias
therefore gates it:

```sh
tamias install --allow-drivers <ref>
# or export TAMIAS_ALLOW_DRIVERS=1 once
```

Without consent the install **fails before anything is registered or
executed** — no partial store entry, no copied driver. Only regular
files directly under `drivers/` are registered, into
`<tamias-home>/drivers/`, where tamias discovers them.

```
mypkg/
  tamias.yaml         # type: myco-config
  drivers/
    tamias-driver-myco
```

## What if there's no driver?

A package whose `type:` has no discoverable driver **fails to install**
(any type other than `files`). tamias never silently "installs" content
it can't place — so either ship the driver, publish
`tamias-driver-<type>` on the host's `PATH`, or use `type: files`.

`tamias deploy`/`uninstall` behave the same way: they dispatch to the
driver for the package's type and warn when none exists.

## Trust boundary

Your driver binary runs with **full user privileges** over an
**untrusted `--dir` payload** — the payload came from a package ref you
may not control. Treat everything under `--dir` as hostile:

* **Never execute payload files yourself.** If the payload ships a
  script or binary, running it is the payload's privilege escalation,
  not yours.
* **Validate every path** you read or write — reject `..` traversal,
  absolute paths, and symlink escapes before touching the filesystem.
* **Don't trust manifest-declared paths or names** — a manifest is
  package-controlled data, not an instruction from the operator.

The consent gates (`--allow-drivers` / `TAMIAS_ALLOW_DRIVERS=1` /
per-package consent memory) decide whether tamias *registers* a bundled
driver — they are **not a sandbox**. Your driver is the last line of
defense.

## Check

```sh
tamias drivers          # every discovered driver + its capabilities
tamias drivers --json   # same, machine-readable
tamias doctor --json    # lists discovered drivers among the health checks
```

## Beyond the lifecycle: pavo surfaces

The lifecycle three plus `capabilities` are the *tamias* contract.
Drivers built on `pavo-driver-kit` additionally answer the **pavo**
surface — `manifest`, `serve` (ndjson views/queries), `ops` (an ops
manifest of bounded verbs), and `run`/`cli` passthroughs — which is how
product CLIs become generatable surfaces: `tamias-driver-tamias`
itself exposes the whole `tamias` engine this way (`cli.<verb>` ops
derived from the clap tree; unbounded verbs like `serve`/`ui` are
`surfaces`, never ops — see
[Scripting tamias](/reference/scripting#the-engine-as-an-ops-manifest)).
A `capabilities` answer of `{"capabilities": ["pavo"], …}` marks a
driver as pavo-capable; `types: []` keeps it from claiming content
types it doesn't handle.

## See also

* [Content types](/explanation/content-types)
* [Provision and service](/how-to/provision-a-service)

url: /tamias/reference/cli.md

# tamias CLI

```
Package & content manager — fetch, store, cache, dispense

Usage: tamias [COMMAND]

Commands:
  install          Fetch → store a package from a ref
  add              Install a ref and record it in `tamias.yaml` + `tamias.lock`
  sync             Reconcile the cwd project's dep set against the store — install what's missing or drifted. Never removes store entries: the store is global, not project-scoped; `tamias remove` stays the uninstall verb
  remove           Drop a store entry (cache untouched)
  list             List installed packages
  info             Show one package's manifest + provenance
  verify           Digest-check a package against its record
  update           Re-resolve + re-install a package from its recorded ref
  pin              Retarget an installed package's recorded source ref
  self-upgrade     Update the tamias package this binary belongs to
  bin              Manage a package's executable surfaces — the declared `bins[]` (generated `cli` shims + `tools/bin/<triple>/` payloads) and `bin/` payload files — on the bin dir (`$TAMIAS_BIN_DIR` → `XDG_BIN_HOME` → `~/.local/bin`)
  cache            Fetch-cache maintenance
  version          Print the tamias version
  manifest         Print the machine-readable capability manifest
  schema           Print the `tamias.yaml` JSON Schema
  gen-cli-docs     Print the CLI reference (markdown) generated from the parser
  completions      Print a shell completion script
  doctor           Diagnose the host metaservice (store, cache, registry, drivers)
  config           Show the effective config — YAML (`tamias.yml`) is the standard
  serve            Run the ndjson JSON-RPC service over stdio
  publish          Publish a package dir to a registry
  search           Search a registry's index
  bundle           Author-side packing
  registry         Registry operations — named sources in the config file
  deploy-registry  Deploy the registry Worker (Cloudflare)
  deploy           Deploy an installed package's service/runtime (via its provider)
  uninstall        Uninstall — provider teardown + drop the store entry
  service          Manage a per-user service unit (systemd)
  drivers          List discovered content drivers (`tamias-driver-<type>` on PATH + `<tamias-home>/drivers/`)
  driver           Provider-verb dispatch — run a driver verb beyond the lifecycle three (`install`/`deploy`/`uninstall`)
  provider         Provider packages — the declarative `provider:` runtime spec
  run              Run an installed provider service's exec in the foreground — the unit's argv + env, without systemd. `tamias run <pkg> [service] [-- extra-args]`
  logs             Follow a package's provider units' journals — `tamias logs <pkg|unit>`. A package name resolves to all its provider units; anything else is treated as a unit base name
  ui               Interactive package-manager TUI (ratatui) — installed entries, registry search, provider lifecycle, manifest deps, authoring
  help             Print this message or the help of the given subcommand(s)

Options:
  -h, --help
          Print help

  -V, --version
          Print version

```

# Ref grammar

A **ref** names *where* a package comes from. One grammar covers all
sources; the impl is picked by shape.

```
./dir                                         local (dev loop)
git:9aia/bupha//libraries/ci-gate#main   git + in-repo subdir + ref
https://…/ci-gate-0.2.0.tgz#sha256:<hex>        tarball (+ digest pin)
cf:<account>/<bucket>/<name>@<ver>             Cloudflare registry
9aia:<name>@<ver>                              named registry (config)
9aia:@scope/<name>@<ver>                        named registry, scoped
```

## Git

* `//subdir` splits the repo from the in-repo path (go-getter
  convention) — required because nested groups make bare `a/b/c/d`
  ambiguous. Without `//`, a two-segment prefix is the repo and the
  remainder is the in-repo path.
* `#ref` is a branch, tag, sha, or **relative rev** (`HEAD~2`, `main^`)
  — the version pin. The resolved commit sha is recorded in the store
  regardless. Revs can't start with `-` or contain whitespace, `..`, or
  `//`, so a ref can't smuggle git options.
* Clone URLs are allowlisted: `https`, `http`, `ssh`, `git`, `file`,
  and scp-style `git@host:…`. Anything else is rejected.
* Fetches run with `GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0` — a credential prompt fails
  the fetch instead of hanging.
* `org/repo` defaults to `github.com`; `host/org/repo` becomes
  `https://host/org/repo`; `git@host:…` and `ssh://`/`file://` pass
  through.

## HTTP

* A `.tgz` / `.tar.gz` URL over `http(s)`, with an optional
  `#sha256:<hex>` pin — verified against the downloaded bytes before
  unpack. An `http://` URL **without** a pin fetches cleartext and
  prints a warning; prefer `https://` or pin the digest.

## Cloudflare registry

```
cf:<account>/<bucket…>/<name>@<version>
```

The address derives the base URL: a full `http(s)://…` passes through
(local / dev registries), a first segment with **no dot** is a
`workers.dev` subdomain, and later segments are a path prefix.

```
cf:9aia/myrepo/ci-gate@0.2.0        → https://9aia.workers.dev/myrepo
cf:reg.example.com/ci-gate@0.2.0    → https://reg.example.com
cf:http://127.0.0.1:8903/w@1.0.0    → http://127.0.0.1:8903
```

`install` fetches `<base>/index.json`, finds `name@version`, pulls the
tarball (`<base>/<file>`), unpacks it, and **verifies the unpacked
payload against the index's recorded `dir_digest`** — a mismatched
payload fails the install. Note the digest covers the payload *dir*, not
the tarball bytes, so it can't be checked at transport (see
[Security model](/explanation/security)).

## Named registry

```
<label>:<name>@<version>
<label>:@scope/<name>@<version>
```

`<label>` resolves against the *effective* config's `registries` map —
the user-level `~/.config/tamias/tamias.*` base overlaid by the cwd
`tamias.*` (same layering as `publish`/`search`). An entry's `id`
(uuid or slug-safe string, `registry add --id`) matches **before** the
map key, so refs can pin a stable id across renames. Only `http`/`cf`
kind registries are installable — a `local` (unserved dir) registry
errors with a pointer at `tamias registry serve`. An unknown label is
a hard error (`unknown registry '<label>'`), never a silent path
fallback.

```
tamias install 9aia:cicada-demo@0.1.0
tamias install 018f3c2e-…:@acme/scoped@2.0.0
```

`@<version>` is required — there is no "latest" resolution. Fetching
goes through the same path as `cf:` (index lookup → payload-digest +
signature verification → tarball fetch), and the store record keeps
the verbatim `<label>:…` ref as provenance. Bearer auth uses the
registry's `token_env` (env var *name*, falling back to
`TAMIAS_REGISTRY_TOKEN`). A `<label>:` that matches a reserved kind
prefix (`git:`, `cf:`, `http(s):`, `ssh:`, `fs:`, `file:`) is never a
registry ref, and single-letter labels are excluded so Windows drive
letters (`C:\…`) can't false-positive.

The same refs work in a project manifest's `deps:` — `tamias sync`
reconciles them like any other ref.

## Local

* `./x`, `../x`, `~/x`, `/x`, or a bare path.

---

---
url: /tamias/reference/config.md
---
# Config — `tamias.yml` / `tamias.yaml` / `tamias.toml`

## `store` / `cache` — an install/fetch location

| field | type | required | notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `kind` | `string` | optional | Impl kind — `local` (default) or `cf`. |
| `root` | `string` | optional | Root dir (or URL base for `cf`). |

## `registries.NAME` — a named registry

| field | type | required | notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `id` | `string` | optional | Stable identifier (typically a uuid) — registry-scoped install refs (`&lt;label&gt;:&lt;name&gt;@&lt;version&gt;`) match `id` before the map key (`name`), so an entry can be renamed without breaking refs that pin the id. Must be ref-label-safe (`[a-zA-Z0-9][a-zA-Z0-9_.-]*`) to be usable in a ref. |
| `kind` | `string` | optional | Explicit kind — `local` | `http` | `cf`. Unset → inferred from `url` (http(s) → `http`, anything else → `local`), so configs written before kinds were explicit keep working. |
| `url` | `string` | optional | Base URL (http) or root dir. |
| `token_env` | `string` | optional | Env var **name** holding the bearer token — never the token. |
| `limits` | `Limits` | optional | Per-registry limit overrides (values + package rules). |
| `retention` | `Retention` | optional | Per-registry retention overrides — how many of a package's most recent versions stay indexed after publish (P-024). |

## `[publish]` — publish routing

| field | type | required | notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `default` | `string` | optional | Registry name `publish` targets by default. |

## `[signing]` — package signing policy

| field | type | required | notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `key` | `string` | optional | Private key path for `publish --sign` (`~` expands) — used when `$TAMIAS_SIGNING_KEY` and `key_env`'s var are unset. |
| `key_env` | `string` | optional | Env var **name** whose value is the signing-key path — checked after `$TAMIAS_SIGNING_KEY`, before `key`. |
| `allowed_signers` | `string` | optional | `allowed_signers` file (authorized_keys-style, principal = `@scope/name` for scoped packages, else the bare name — with a bare-name fallback) for signature verification. `$TAMIAS_ALLOWED_SIGNERS` wins; default `~/.config/tamias/allowed_signers`. |
| `official_signers` | `string` | optional | `official_signers` file — the smaller trust set backing the official-badge check. `$TAMIAS_OFFICIAL_SIGNERS` wins; default `~/.config/tamias/official_signers`. |
| `required` | `bool` | optional | Every install must carry a valid signature. Only registry (`cf:`) refs can supply one — see `tamias-sign`'s docs. |
| `namespace` | `string` | optional | `ssh-keygen -Y` namespace (default `tamias-package`). |

## `[retention]` — publish retention (P-024)

| field | type | required | notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `keep` | `int` | optional | Versions kept per package — `0` keeps only the just-published version. `None` inherits the next level / disables pruning. |
| `packages` | `BTreeMap<String, Retention>` | required | Per-package overrides — exact name or `*` glob → retention. Lives on the global `retention` (and may appear under a registry's `retention`); `packages` nested inside a package entry is ignored — overrides are one level deep. |

## Top level

| field | type | required | notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `store` | `Location` | optional | Install store location — `root` applies when `kind` is `local`/unset and `TAMIAS_HOME`/XDG env is unset (env wins). |
| `cache` | `Location` | optional | Fetch-cache location — same resolution rule as `store`. |
| `registries` | `BTreeMap<String, Registry>` | optional | Named registries — `publish`/`search --registry &lt;name&gt;` and the `publish.default`/`search.default` routing resolve through these; registry-scoped install refs (`&lt;label&gt;:&lt;name&gt;@&lt;version&gt;`) match an entry's `id` first, then its map key. |
| `publish` | `Publish` | optional | Publish routing. |
| `search` | `Search` | optional | Search routing. |
| `limits` | `Limits` | optional | Global byte limits + per-package overrides. |
| `retention` | `Retention` | optional | Global retention policy — versions kept per package after publish (P-024). Unset → no pruning. |
| `signing` | `Signing` | optional | Package signing policy — `publish --sign` key resolution and install/verify `allowed_signers`/`official_signers` enforcement and trust-tier reporting (`tamias-sign`). |

## format trait (parse/render)

| field | type | required | notes |
|---|---|---|---|

## Formats

YAML is the standard — `tamias.yml` or `tamias.yaml`; `tamias.toml`
parses into the same `Config`. Read-side resolution is **layered**:
the user-level `~/.config/tamias/tamias.*` (`$XDG_CONFIG_HOME`
wins) is the base and a `./tamias.{yml,yaml,toml}` in the cwd
overlays it per-field — project wins, global fills the gaps.
`--file`/`TAMIAS_CONFIG` replaces discovery with that one file.
Registry *writes* (`tamias registry add|remove`) stay file-scoped:
they edit the project `tamias.*` (or `--file` target), never the
user layer implicitly. The merged config informs `doctor`'s
registry check (`publish.default` → `registries.NAME`).

## Constraints

* Token values never live in the file — `token_env` fields name
  the env var that carries them (the http client reads
  `TAMIAS_REGISTRY_TOKEN`).
* `tamias config --json` dumps the effective config;
  `tamias schema` emits the JSON Schema for the *package* manifest
  (`tamias.yaml`), a different document.

url: /tamias/reference/scripting.md
---
# Scripting tamias

Everything an agent or CI job needs without scraping human output.

## `--json`

These verbs emit JSON with `--json`:

| verb | shape |
| --- | --- |
| `list` | `{"packages": [entry…]}` — record fields + `label`, `size`, `dir` |
| `info <name>` | one entry object (same fields) |
| `verify <name>` | `{name, recorded, computed, ok, signature, trust, signer}` — non-zero exit on mismatch |
| `update [name]` | `{"updated": [label…]}` (with `--all` or a name) |
| `doctor` | per-check report — store, cache, git, registry, drivers |
| `config` | `{file, search, config}` — the effective config |
| `search <q>` | `{"results": [{label, name, scope, version, kind, digest, signed, publisher, file}]}` |
| `cache clean` | `{evicted, entries}` |

Without `--json` the same verbs print aligned text.

## Capability discovery

```sh
tamias manifest      # {"name","version","verbs":[…]} — verbs generated from the parser
tamias schema        # JSON Schema for the package manifest (tamias.yaml)
tamias gen-cli-docs  # this CLI reference, regenerated from clap
tamias completions bash|zsh|fish|elvish|powershell
```

`manifest`'s verb list can't drift — it's generated from the clap tree
each run.

## `tamias serve`

For stateful, interactive use, `tamias serve` speaks ndjson JSON-RPC
over stdio — see [the serve reference](/reference/serve).

## The engine as an ops manifest

`tamias-driver-tamias` (installed with tamias, discovered like any
driver) exposes the whole `tamias` CLI as a **pavo ops manifest** —
every bounded verb as a `cli.<verb>` wire query derived from the
engine's own clap tree, so generated surfaces (pavo's CLI/MCP
renderers) can't drift from the real verbs. Unbounded surfaces
(`serve`, `ui`, `registry serve`, `run`) are listed as `surfaces`,
never ops. Drive it over the driver's `serve` wire:

```sh
tamias-driver-tamias serve <<'EOF'
{"op":"query","query":"ops"}
{"op":"query","query":"cli.list","params":{}}
EOF
```

`query:"cli.<verb>"` params map by kind — `arg` = positional,
`opt` = `--name <v>`, `flag` = `--name`. `tamias-driver-tamias run <argv…>` is the raw passthrough (`run list` ≡ `tamias list`). Secret
params should ride stdin, not argv — generated CLIs accept
`--params-stdin` (a JSON object merged over the flags) so tokens stay
out of shell history.

## Environment

| var | effect |
| --- | --- |
| `TAMIAS_HOME` | store + `drivers/` root (default `~/.local/share/tamias`) |
| `TAMIAS_CACHE` | fetch-cache root (default `~/.cache/tamias/fetch`) |
| `TAMIAS_BIN_DIR` | bin dir for `tamias bin` deploys (default `$XDG_BIN_HOME` → `~/.local/bin`) |
| `TAMIAS_REGISTRY` | default registry root for `publish`/`search` |
| `TAMIAS_CONFIG` | explicit config file — replaces discovery for that invocation |
| `TAMIAS_ALLOW_DRIVERS` | `=1` consents to bundled `drivers/` (same as `--allow-drivers`) |
| `TAMIAS_CONSENT_FILE` | override the per-package driver-consent memory path |
| `TAMIAS_REGISTRY_TOKEN` | bearer token for http(s) registries |
| `TAMIAS_REGISTRY_SERVE_TOKEN` | require auth on `tamias registry serve` |
| `TAMIAS_SIGNING_KEY` / `TAMIAS_ALLOWED_SIGNERS` / `TAMIAS_OFFICIAL_SIGNERS` | `publish --sign` key + signature-trust files (names, never values inline) |
| `TAMIAS_OTEL_*` / `OTEL_*` | opt-in telemetry — see [Architecture](/explanation/architecture#observability) |

Config discovery is **layered**: the user-level
`~/.config/tamias/tamias.{yml,yaml,toml}` is the base and a
`./tamias.{yml,yaml,toml}` in the cwd overlays it per-field — project
wins, global fills the gaps. `--file`/`TAMIAS_CONFIG` replaces
discovery with that one file. Registry *writes* (`tamias registry
add|remove`) stay file-scoped — they edit the project `tamias.*` (or
`--file` target), never the user layer implicitly.

## Exit codes

A failed verb exits non-zero. `verify` fails on digest mismatch;
`doctor` fails if any check fails (the report still prints first).
`cache clean --all` and `--days` conflict — pick one.

---

---
url: /tamias/reference/serve.md
---
# `tamias serve` — JSON-RPC over stdio

`tamias serve` runs tamias as an **ndjson JSON-RPC service**: one JSON
request per line on stdin, one JSON response per line on stdout. It's
the embedding surface — a parent process (an agent harness, a daemon)
drives installs without shelling out per verb.

## Framing

Request:  `{"op": "<op>", …fields}`
Response: `{"ok": true, "result": …}` or `{"ok": false, "error": "…"}`

A failed op returns `ok:false` — it does not kill the service. The
service exits when stdin closes.

## Ops

| op | fields | result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `install` | `ref`, `allow_drivers?` | `{label, resolved, digest, signed}` |
| `plan` | `ref`, `allow_drivers?` | the `tamias install --plan` report — manifest, cache hit, payload digest, classified `include:`s, bundled drivers + consent need, kind driver, provider services, `trust`/`signer`/`signature_status`, `problems`. Dry-run: nothing is committed or dispatched |
| `sync` | `locked?`, `from_lock?`, `allow_drivers?`, `dir?` | `{deps: [{dep, status, detail}], failed}` — reconciles the project manifest's `deps:` against the store + `tamias.lock` (`dir` defaults to the server's cwd; `from_lock: true` makes `tamias.lock` itself the spec, like `tamias sync --from-lock`) |
| `list` | — | `[{label, source_ref, digest}]` |
| `info` | `name` | `{label, resolved, digest, size}` |
| `verify` | `name` | `{name, ok, signature, trust, signer}` — `trust`/`signer` are re-derived live, same rule as `tamias verify` |
| `remove` | `name` | `{name}` — runs driver teardown first, like `tamias uninstall` |
| `search` | `query`, `registry?` | `{results: [{label, name, scope, version, kind, digest, signed, publisher, file}]}` |
| `publish` | `dir`, `registry?`, `keep_includes?`, `keep?`, `sign?` | `{label, name, scope, version, kind, digest, signed, publisher, file, pruned}` — `keep` is the per-invocation retention override (P-024), `sign: true` attaches an ssh signature (`publish --sign`) |
| `registry.list` | — | `{registries: [{name, id, kind, effective_kind, url, token_env, limits, retention}]}` |
| `registry.get` | `name` | one registry object (same shape as `registry.list` items) |
| `registry.add` | `name`, `kind`, `url`, `token_env?`, `id?` | `{name, config}` — writes the config file |
| `registry.remove` | `name` | `{name, config}` |

`name` accepts `@scope/name` or bare `name`, same as the CLI.

`install` does **not** deploy `bins[]` — bin deployment is a
CLI-side post-commit step (`tamias install`'s default pass /
`tamias bin deploy`) that the serve ops don't run. A serve-driven
install of a bins\[] pack leaves the store entry committed but the
commands undeployed until something calls `tamias bin deploy <pkg>`.
(The `sync` op shares this — and so does the CLI's own `tamias sync`,
which installs through `tamias-install` without the bin pass.)

`search`/`publish` take `registry` as a **name or raw ref** — identical
resolution to `--registry` on the CLI verbs: config `registries` name →
raw dir/http ref → routing defaults (`search.default` →
`publish.default`) → `TAMIAS_REGISTRY` env → the local default root.
`registry.add`/`remove` write `tamias.{yml,yaml,toml}` through the same
path as `tamias registry add|remove`; `token_env` is an env var *name*,
never a token value.

## Driver consent

`install` refuses payload-shipped `drivers/` unless the request carries
`"allow_drivers": true` (or `TAMIAS_ALLOW_DRIVERS=1` is set) — identical
to `--allow-drivers`. Bundled drivers are never registered or executed
without it; once consented, the grant is remembered per package +
payload digest in `consented.json` (see
[Security model](/explanation/security)).

## Trust boundary

**Stdin is fully trusted.** Any process that can write to the service's
stdin can pass `"allow_drivers": true` and reach every op — there is no
per-request authentication. Embed `tamias serve` only behind a harness
that has already made the trust decision; never expose it to untrusted
input.

## Environment

The service honors the same roots as the CLI: `TAMIAS_HOME` (store +
`drivers/`), `TAMIAS_CACHE`, `TAMIAS_REGISTRY`, `TAMIAS_CONFIG` (the
config file `registry.*` ops read/write and `search`/`publish` resolve
against — re-read per request, so writes are visible in-session), and
the telemetry vars (`TAMIAS_OTEL_*`).

## Example

```sh
printf '%s\n' \
  '{"op":"install","ref":"./hello"}' \
  '{"op":"list"}' \
  '{"op":"verify","name":"hello"}' \
| tamias serve
```

## See also

* [Scripting tamias](/reference/scripting) — `--json`, `manifest`, `schema`
* [Security model](/explanation/security)

# Crate API

Rustdoc for every workspace crate — public APIs are
documented at source (doc comments).

* [tamias-core](/tamias/api/tamias_core/index.html) — domain
* [tamias-cache](/tamias/api/tamias_cache/index.html) — port
