# Architecture

> Seeded from a copy of `cuora` (its ports-and-adapters anatomy and the
> `-cf` Worker pattern).

tamias is **ports-and-adapters**. The engine owns the generic half of
distribution; every content *meaning* is an adapter.

## Ports

| Port | Role | Impls |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `ref` | claims + parses a ref into an opaque spec | one per kind (in the `source-*` crates) |
| `source` | `plan(spec)` → `fetch(plan, into)` | `-fs`, `-git`, `-http`, `-cf` |
| `store` | put/get/verify an installed package | `-local`, `-cf` |
| `cache` | content-addressed fetch cache | `-local`, `-cf` |
| `registry` | index + publish | `-local`, `-cf` (Worker + R2 + D1/KV) |
| `deploy` | service unit + teardown | `-systemd` (Linux), `-launchd` (macOS), `-windows` (Task Scheduler), `-cf` (registry Worker) |
| `driver` | how a content *type* installs/deploys | `tamias-driver-<type>` (subprocess, argv) |

## Crate map

| crate | layer | purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `tamias-core` | domain | Pure domain — package identity (@scope/name@semver), refs, manifests, records, digests (no I/O) |
| `tamias-cache` | port | cache port — read-through fetched content |
| `tamias-config` | port | Config port — where tamias.toml-shaped config comes from |
| `tamias-deploy` | port | deploy port — provision a remote registry (Worker + R2 + D1/KV) |
| `tamias-registry` | port | registry port — index + publish |
| `tamias-source` | port | source port — turn a ref into bytes |
| `tamias-store` | port | store port — content-addressed blobs |
| `tamias-bin` | adapter | Declared bins\[] lifecycle — tools/bin/\<triple> payloads, bin-dir deploy/destroy/list |
| `tamias-cache-cf` | adapter | Cloudflare adapter (P6) |
| `tamias-cache-local` | adapter | local cache impl — content-addressed fetch cache |
| `tamias-config-toml` | adapter | TOML config impl |
| `tamias-config-yml` | adapter | YAML config impl (the standard) — tamias.yml / tamias.yaml |
| `tamias-deploy-cf` | adapter | Cloudflare deploy impl — the registry Worker + wrangler config |
| `tamias-deploy-launchd` | adapter | macos deploy impl — manage a per-user launchd agent (LaunchAgents plist + launchctl) |
| `tamias-deploy-systemd` | adapter | systemd deploy impl — manage a per-user service unit (Linux) |
| `tamias-deploy-windows` | adapter | windows deploy impl — manage a per-user scheduled task (Task Scheduler via schtasks.exe) |
| `tamias-driver` | adapter | content driver host — discovery + dispatch of tamias-driver-\<type> (no product knowledge) |
| `tamias-driver-tamias` | adapter | tamias-driver-tamias — pavo view driver over the tamias install store, fetch cache, registry index, and driver dir (read-only) |
| `tamias-install` | adapter | The shared install pipeline — ref → fetch/cache → manifest → driver dispatch → store commit |
| `tamias-provider` | adapter | provider lifecycle — installed `provider:` blocks → units, deploy/uninstall, run exec specs, journal argv |
| `tamias-publish` | adapter | author side — pack + push |
| `tamias-registry-cf` | adapter | Cloudflare registry impl — a Worker + R2 over HTTP |
| `tamias-registry-local` | adapter | dir registry impl — a folder index, servable over HTTP |
| `tamias-registry-open` | adapter | shared registry-source layer — name-or-ref resolution + named-source config CRUD |
| `tamias-serve` | adapter | ndjson JSON-RPC over stdio — the embedding surface |
| `tamias-shell` | adapter | Run a command in a working directory via bash -c — the generic shell-out helper |
| `tamias-sign` | adapter | Package signing — ssh-keygen -Y sign/verify (namespace tamias-package) over the provenance anchors |
| `tamias-source-cf` | adapter | Cloudflare registry source impl — the `cf:` ref arm |
| `tamias-source-fs` | adapter | fs source impl — local dirs and tarballs |
| `tamias-source-git` | adapter | git source impl — clone URL //subdir #rev |
| `tamias-source-http` | adapter | http source impl — .tgz GET + optional sha256 pin |
| `tamias-source-registry` | adapter | Registry-scoped install refs — the `&lt;registry&gt;:&lt;name&gt;[@&lt;version&gt;]` ref arm |
| `tamias-store-cf` | adapter | Cloudflare adapter (P6) |
| `tamias-store-local` | adapter | local store impl — a directory |
| `tamias-telemetry` | adapter | Opt-in OpenTelemetry layer over the tracing stack — OTLP export, W3C context propagation |
| `tamias-testkit` | adapter | Fixtures + adapter conformance for every port |
| `tamias-tui` | adapter | tamias — interactive package-manager TUI (ratatui); the `tamias ui` surface |
| `tamias` | binary | tamias — package & content manager: fetch, store, cache, dispense |

## The install path

```
ref ─► resolve ─► (cache hit?) ─► fetch ─► driver install ─► store
```

`include:` composes payloads: each entry resolves to a store payload
or a recursively-installed ref, `overlay()` deep-merges bases (earlier
includes win, local wins) and the *composed* tree is what drivers see,
what gets digested, and what the store commits. `publish`/`bundle pack`
flatten includes by default (`--keep-includes` ships the raw payload).

`resolve` pins git refs to a commit sha up front, so the content-
addressed cache can be hit *before* fetching. The fetch→unpack split is
what makes repeat installs and air-gapped nodes free.

Declared `bins[]` (P-023) ride the same commit: every install path —
`install`/`add`/`update`, `sync`, the `tamias serve` `install` op, the
TUI — deploys them into the bin dir by default (`--no-bins` opts out
on the CLI verbs) — `shim: cli`
entries become generated scripts exec'ing `tamias bin exec`, and
`payload: tools/bin/<triple>/…` entries link real binaries through a
per-package `bin-alias/` so upgrades don't break them. `bin/`
payload files link the same way (legacy, undeclared). See
[Put a package's binaries on your PATH](/how-to/link-binaries).

## Stores

* **install store** — `<name>@<version>/` with a record (source ref,
  resolved sha, payload digest, installed-at).
* **fetch cache** — content-addressed; `remove` never touches it.
* **registry** — where published content lives: a directory, or a
  Cloudflare Worker + R2 + D1/KV.

## Provenance

`verify` recomputes the payload digest against the record. Digest-pinned
refs (`#sha256:…`, resolved shas) are the integrity contract — see
[Security model](/explanation/security) for the full trust story,
including the `--allow-drivers` consent gate on payload-shipped drivers.

## The embedding surface

`tamias serve` (the `tamias-serve` crate) runs the same
install/list/info/verify/remove verbs plus the registry surface —
`search`, `publish`, and `registry.list|get|add|remove` — as an
**ndjson JSON-RPC service over stdio** for agents and daemons that want
a persistent handle instead of one-shot CLI calls. Registry name-or-ref
resolution and config writes go through `tamias-registry-open`, the same
code the CLI verbs use. The protocol is specified in
[serve reference](/reference/serve).

A second embedding surface targets **generated** clients:
`tamias-driver-tamias` exposes the engine's clap tree as a pavo ops
manifest (`cli.<verb>` wire queries), so pavo's CLI/MCP renderers drive
the same verbs without a hand-written client — see
[Scripting tamias](/reference/scripting#the-engine-as-an-ops-manifest).

## Observability

`tamias-telemetry` is an opt-in OpenTelemetry layer over the tracing
stack. Nothing exports unless you set an endpoint:

* `TAMIAS_OTEL_ENDPOINT` — OTLP/HTTP base URL (the opt-in switch), or
  the standard `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT` /
  `…_TRACES_ENDPOINT`.
* `TAMIAS_OTEL_SERVICE_NAME` / `OTEL_SERVICE_NAME` — `service.name`.
* W3C `traceparent`/`tracestate` propagation is installed when export
  is on; `RUST_LOG`-style filtering still applies.

---
url: /tamias/explanation/content-types.md
---
# Content types

The engine is **generic**: it moves *bytes + a manifest* and doesn't
care what the bytes mean. A **content type** declares the meaning —
where and how a package installs.

## Declared, not linked

A content type is *data first*: the package's manifest names its `type`
(`kind`). The manager never links a product crate. When a product must do
real work (materialize a node config, enable a systemd unit), it ships a
**driver** binary the manager launches as a subprocess — "no plugin
system: files" (peregrin’s own ADR).

## The roster

| Type | Payload | Installs into |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `peregrin-bundle` | workflows, `.node.yml`, `.snippet.yml`, `.field.yml`, `.prompt.yml` | the peregrin bundle store |
| `myco-config` | `[[kinds]]`, `[views]`, `[verbs]`, templates | `myco.toml` / a seeded `project/` |
| `kuda-domain` | `data/domains/*.toml` | `.kuda/domains/` |
| `mimus-rules` | `rules/*.toml` | `rules/` |
| `files` | anything | the store entry (no driver) |

Adding a type is a new `tamias-driver-<type>` binary — never a change to
the engine.

## Drivers

The engine is generic — it moves *bytes + a manifest* and unpacks into
the store. Everything product-specific beyond that is a **driver**:
when a package's `type:` isn't `files`, tamias resolves a
`tamias-driver-<type>` executable — on `PATH` or in
`<tamias-home>/drivers/` — and runs it as a subprocess:

```text
tamias-driver-<type> install --dir <payload> --name <name> [--config <file>]
tamias-driver-<type> deploy   --dir <dir>     --name <name> [--config <file>]
tamias-driver-<type> uninstall --dir <dir>    --name <name>
tamias-driver-<type> capabilities            # → {"types":[…]}
```

The driver owns the product's schema — where it materializes, what
"deployed" means, how to tear down. tamias never learns it. Drivers
built on `pavo-driver-kit` additionally answer the pavo surface
(`manifest`/`serve`/`ops`/`run`) — views plus an ops manifest of bounded
verbs for generated clients; see
[Write a driver](/how-to/write-a-driver#beyond-the-lifecycle-pavo-surfaces).

A package can **ship its own driver** under `drivers/` in the payload;
installing registers it into `<tamias-home>/drivers/`. Because that's
arbitrary code, it requires `--allow-drivers` /
`TAMIAS_ALLOW_DRIVERS=1` — see [Security model](/explanation/security).

`files` is the built-in type: the store entry is the whole story, no
driver needed. Any other type **fails to install** without a
discoverable driver — fail closed, never silent.

`tamias drivers` lists every discovered driver (PATH +
`<tamias-home>/drivers/`) with its `capabilities` answer — types,
verbs, location — the same scan `doctor` summarizes.

See [Write a driver](/how-to/write-a-driver) for the authoring side.

---

---
url: /tamias/explanation/security.md
---
# Security model

Tamias moves other people's code onto your machine, so the threat model
is **supply chain**: a malicious or tampered package, a hijacked ref, a
poisoned registry. This page explains the layers; `SECURITY.md` at the
repo root is the reporting policy.

## Integrity: digests and pins

Every install records three things in the store entry: the **source
ref**, the **resolved sha** (commit sha for git, payload sha256 for
tarballs), and the **payload digest**. `tamias verify` recomputes the
digest and fails on mismatch — tampering with the store is detected.

Prefer pinned refs:

* `…#sha256:<hex>` on an http tarball — verified *before* unpack.
* git refs resolve to a commit sha up front, so the recorded `resolved`
  is immutable even when the branch moves.
* `cf:` registry installs carry the registry index digest — pinned by
  name@version plus that digest.

Two honest caveats:

* `http://` refs **without** a `#sha256:` pin fetch cleartext and warn
  on stderr. Use `https://` or pin the digest.
* `cf:` registry installs are TLS-authenticated but **not**
  sha-pinned at transport — the registry records a payload *directory*
  digest, not the tarball sha256. For end-to-end integrity prefer `git:`
  or an http ref with `#sha256:`.

Two more warnings worth knowing:

* **`include:` transitive fetches.** A manifest `include:` that names a
  remote ref pulls *another* package at install time — and tamias warns
  when that ref is unpinned (an http(s) ref without `#sha256:`, or a
  `git:` rev that isn't a full 40-hex sha). The warning is advisory:
  remote includes are legitimate, but each one is a second supply-chain
  hop that bypasses whatever pin you put on the top-level ref.
* **Cleartext registry index.** Fetching `index.json` over `http://`
  warns on every call — the index is unauthenticated and modifiable in
  transit, so the payload digests it records are only as trustworthy as
  that GET. Signatures mitigate this *only* when
  `signing.allowed_signers` is configured (see below).

Tarball unpacking is bounded independently of `max_download` (which
caps the compressed blob): every untar enforces a **2 GiB unpacked-size
cap** and a **100k entry cap**, so a tiny `.tgz` can't expand into disk
or inode exhaustion. Manifest `type:`/`kind` strings are charset-validated
(`[a-z0-9][a-z0-9._-]*`) because the kind becomes `tamias-driver-<kind>`
in binary lookups — it can't smuggle path or option characters.

## Trust tiers: provenance, computed not declared

Signing is optional package signing (`ssh-keygen -Y`, namespace
`tamias-package`) — `publish --sign` attaches a signature, `tamias-sign`
verifies it. On top of raw signature status, every install and verify
computes a **trust tier** and records it on the store entry (`trust` +
`signer` fields):

| tier | meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `official` | signature verifies against `signing.official_signers` — the small, curated trust set |
| `signed` | signature verifies against `signing.allowed_signers`, but not the official set |
| `pinned` | no verifiable signature, but the source ref carries an integrity pin (`cf:`, `#sha256:`, a full git sha) |
| `unpinned` | no signature and no pin — a moving branch/tag, bare http(s), a local path |
| `bad` | a signature is present and verification **failed** — a failed signature is never shown as merely unsigned |

The tier is *computed* from the ref, the signature, and your signers
files — a package can't declare its own badge. Highest wins: an official
signature short-circuits before `allowed_signers` is even consulted, and
a present-but-failed signature beats any pin.

Where it surfaces:

* `tamias list` — a `trust` column.
* `tamias info` / `tamias verify` — `trust` + `signer`; `--json` carries
  the same fields, and `verify` re-derives the tier live (a recorded
  signer wins, but a rotated `allowed_signers` file is honored).
* `tamias search` / `registry get` / `tamias serve` `verify` —
  `trust`/`signer`/`publisher` fields.
* `tamias ui` — trust badges.
* `tamias doctor` — reports the resolved `official_signers` path.

### Bootstrapping `official_signers`

`allowed_signers` and `official_signers` are **two different files**:
the first says "this key may sign packages I install"; the second is the
smaller set that earns the `official` badge — think "keys we ship under"
versus "keys we merely tolerate". Resolution order for each (env wins):

| file | config | env | default |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| allowed | `signing.allowed_signers` | `TAMIAS_ALLOWED_SIGNERS` | `~/.config/tamias/allowed_signers` |
| official | `signing.official_signers` | `TAMIAS_OFFICIAL_SIGNERS` | `~/.config/tamias/official_signers` |

Both are `ssh-keygen -Y` `allowed_signers` files (authorized_keys
format, principals + keys). To mint an official identity:

```sh
ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -f ~/.ssh/tamias-official
# sign a package with it (key path resolution: $TAMIAS_SIGNING_KEY →
# signing.key_env → signing.key):
TAMIAS_SIGNING_KEY=~/.ssh/tamias-official tamias publish --sign ./mypkg
# authorize the *public* key for the package's signing principal —
# `@scope/name` for a scoped package, the bare `name` for unscoped:
echo 'mypkg namespaces="tamias-package" ssh-ed25519 AAAA…' \
  >> ~/.config/tamias/official_signers
```

Signing principals are **scoped**: a package `@scope/name` is signed and
verified under the principal `@scope/name`; an unscoped package falls
back to the bare `name` (and legacy records keep working the same way).
`signing.required` additionally makes unsigned installs a hard error —
but only `cf:`/registry refs can carry signatures, so `required` is a
registry-policy switch; `tamias doctor` warns when `required` is set
without a resolvable `allowed_signers`.

## Drivers are code — consent is explicit, remembered per payload

A package's `type:` names a **driver** (`tamias-driver-<type>`), which
tamias executes as a subprocess. Drivers on `PATH` or in
`<tamias-home>/drivers/` are trusted host tooling.

A package that **ships its own `drivers/` dir** is different: those
binaries are arbitrary code inside the payload. Installing one requires
explicit consent:

```sh
tamias install --allow-drivers <ref>
# or once per environment:
TAMIAS_ALLOW_DRIVERS=1 tamias install <ref>
```

`TAMIAS_ALLOW_DRIVERS=1` is a **global bypass** — it covers every
install, including ones you haven't inspected; `tamias doctor` warns
when it's set. Prefer `--allow-drivers` per install, or better, check
the package first with `--plan`.

**`tamias install --plan`** is the pre-flight check: a dry run that
prints the ref, package identity, cache hit/miss, payload digest,
trust tier + signer, signature status, `include:` resolutions, bundled
drivers with their consent state, the resolved kind driver, provider
services (deploy-only), and any problems — **without executing drivers,
committing to the store, or mutating anything**. `--plan --json` gives
the same picture machine-readably. It runs `capabilities` probes on
discovered drivers (trusted local binaries), so it's safe to point at a
ref you don't trust yet.

Consent is also **remembered per package**: after a granted install,
tamias records `{label → payload digest, drivers, timestamp}` in
`~/.config/tamias/consented.json` (`$TAMIAS_CONSENT_FILE` /
`$XDG_CONFIG_HOME/tamias/` override the path). Re-installing the *same
bytes* skips re-consent; a changed payload produces a new digest and
re-prompts — consent binds to exact content, not to the package name.
The memory is shared across surfaces: the CLI flag/env, the `tamias
serve` `"allow_drivers": true` request field, and the TUI consent modal
all write the same file.

Without consent the install **fails before anything is registered or
run** — no partial store entry, no copied driver.

**Executable surfaces are a separate, ungated channel.** A package's
`bins[]` (`payload:` entries under `tools/bin/`) and legacy `bin/`
files deploy real binaries onto your `PATH` at install time with **no
consent prompt** — the `--allow-drivers` gate covers `drivers/` only.
A `shim: cli` entry is safe by construction (a generated script that
execs `tamias bin exec`), but treat any pack that declares payload
bins like you would a driver: inspect before installing
(`tamias install --plan` lists declared bins).

## Missing drivers fail closed

Installing a package whose `type` has **no** discoverable driver fails
the install (for any type other than `files`) — tamias never silently
"installs" content it can't place. `tamias doctor` lists the drivers it
found so you can see what's resolvable.

## Secrets are names, never values

* Registry tokens live in env vars — `TAMIAS_REGISTRY_TOKEN` for http
  registries, or the env var *named* by a config `token_env` field.
  `tamias.yaml` / `tamias.lock` hold refs, names, and digests only.
* `tamias registry serve` is an open dev server unless you set
  `TAMIAS_REGISTRY_SERVE_TOKEN` (then every request needs
  `Authorization: Bearer …`).

## `tamias serve` trusts its stdin

The ndjson service treats **everything on stdin as trusted**: an
`install` op can pass `"allow_drivers": true` — equivalent to
`--allow-drivers` — and there's no per-request authentication. Embed it
only behind a harness that has already made the trust decision; never
expose `tamias serve` to untrusted input.

## Git fetch hardening

* Clone URLs are allowlisted: `https`, `http`, `ssh`, `git`, `file`,
  and scp-style `git@host:…`. Other schemes are rejected.
* Revs are validated — no leading `-`, whitespace, `..`, or `//`, so a
  ref can't smuggle git options. Relative revs (`HEAD~2`, `main^`) are
  allowed.
* `GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0` — a fetch never blocks on a credential
  prompt; it fails instead.

## Reporting

Vulnerabilities go to the maintainers via GitHub private advisories —
see `SECURITY.md`. Don't open public issues for security reports.

---

---
url: /tamias/explanation/boundaries.md
---
# Boundaries

Tamias owns **content distribution**: refs, transport, the install store

* fetch cache, and content-type dispatch. Every neighbour owns its own
  concern.

| Sibling | Owns | Relationship |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **peregrin** | orchestration | `install/remove/list/…` become thin wrappers over `tamias-*`; peregrin's distribution impl moves here |
| **myco** | work memory | kinds/views/templates ship as a `myco-config` content type |
| **kuda** | code memory | `kuda-domain` packs |
| **mimus** | critic | `mimus-rules` packs |
| **cuora** | secrets | publish tokens / private-registry creds via `cuora://` refs |
| **sturn** | coordination | claim the store lock during concurrent installs |
| **bupha / ci-gate** | CI gate | bupha is the CI repo — `type: bupha` bundles via `tamias-driver-bupha`; the org gate is mid-migration back from the peregrin `ci-gate` campaign (PL-013) |
| **sepia** | sessions | — |
| **cicada** | calendars | `type: cicada` bundles via `tamias-driver-cicada` (install validates, deploy plans — apply stays cicada's gate); `tamias update --all` + registry reindex |

A hosted registry is in scope (it's a `registry` impl). A daemon or
multi-actor arbitration belongs to peregrin.

## SIL OPEN FONT LICENSE Version 1.1 - 26 February 2007

PREAMBLE
The goals of the Open Font License (OFL) are to stimulate worldwide
development of collaborative font projects, to support the font creation
efforts of academic and linguistic communities, and to provide a free and
open framework in which fonts may be shared and improved in partnership
with others.

The OFL allows the licensed fonts to be used, studied, modified and
redistributed freely as long as they are not sold by themselves. The
fonts, including any derivative works, can be bundled, embedded,
redistributed and/or sold with any software provided that any reserved
names are not used by derivative works. The fonts and derivatives,
however, cannot be released under any other type of license. The
requirement for fonts to remain under this license does not apply
to any document created using the fonts or their derivatives.

DEFINITIONS
"Font Software" refers to the set of files released by the Copyright
Holder(s) under this license and clearly marked as such. This may
include source files, build scripts and documentation.

"Reserved Font Name" refers to any names specified as such after the
copyright statement(s).

"Original Version" refers to the collection of Font Software components as
distributed by the Copyright Holder(s).

"Modified Version" refers to any derivative made by adding to, deleting,
or substituting -- in part or in whole -- any of the components of the
Original Version, by changing formats or by porting the Font Software to a
new environment.

"Author" refers to any designer, engineer, programmer, technical
writer or other person who contributed to the Font Software.

PERMISSION & CONDITIONS
Permission is hereby granted, free of charge, to any person obtaining
a copy of the Font Software, to use, study, copy, merge, embed, modify,
redistribute, and sell modified and unmodified copies of the Font
Software, subject to the following conditions:

1. Neither the Font Software nor any of its individual components,
   in Original or Modified Versions, may be sold by itself.

2. Original or Modified Versions of the Font Software may be bundled,
   redistributed and/or sold with any software, provided that each copy
   contains the above copyright notice and this license. These can be
   included either as stand-alone text files, human-readable headers or
   in the appropriate machine-readable metadata fields within text or
   binary files as long as those fields can be easily viewed by the user.

3. No Modified Version of the Font Software may use the Reserved Font
   Name(s) unless explicit written permission is granted by the corresponding
   Copyright Holder. This restriction only applies to the primary font name as
   presented to the users.

4. The name(s) of the Copyright Holder(s) or the Author(s) of the Font
   Software shall not be used to promote, endorse or advertise any
   Modified Version, except to acknowledge the contribution(s) of the
   Copyright Holder(s) and the Author(s) or with their explicit written
   permission.

5. The Font Software, modified or unmodified, in part or in whole,
   must be distributed entirely under this license, and must not be
   distributed under any other license. The requirement for fonts to
   remain under this license does not apply to any document created
   using the Font Software.

TERMINATION
This license becomes null and void if any of the above conditions are
not met.
